query: Consider noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing more than five elements and targeted in a single-phase solid-solution state. Their crystal structure is difficult to control at fixed composition, while unsuccessful formation can involve phase separation, elemental segregation, uncontrolled particle morphology, and high thermal decomposition temperatures under synthesis regimes with rapid heating and cooling. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs formation and crystal-structure selection in this regime and why? Define a controlled intervention without specifying a technique, predict the observations relative to the initial single-phase baseline, identify the applicable compositional and processing boundaries, cite supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In rapid high-temperature synthesis of noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles with more than five elements, the formation of a single-phase solid solution is governed primarily by kinetic trapping combined with statistical dilution. Because rapid heating and ultra‐fast cooling severely limit atomic mobility, atoms are locked into a disordered, randomly mixed state despite potentially unfavorable binary interactions. In multicomponent systems, the low local concentration of any one type minimizes the chance for elemental clustering or ordering. A slight intentional increase in the dwell time at peak temperature would then enable enough mobility for local segregation or the formation of secondary phases, demonstrating that the process is fundamentally controlled by the interplay between limited diffusion (kinetic effects) and stochastic mixing from high elemental diversity.
generation.material_initial_state: A solid precursor film or mixture of noble metal salt precursors (comprising more than five elements) deposited on a carbon-based support, which when subjected to rapid Joule heating yields kinetically trapped, uniformly mixed HEA nanoparticles.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled extension of the dwell time at the peak synthesis temperature (for example, increasing the time at ~1100 K from tens of milliseconds to a few seconds) without altering the overall high temperature or the rapid cooling rate.
generation.conditions: Synthesis under inert atmosphere (e.g., argon) with rapid heating to around 1100 K and typical cooling rates of 10^4 to 10^5 K/s, where the sole change is the increased dwell time at the peak temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of atomic mixing and the limited diffusion length during precursor reduction, which determines whether atoms remain randomly dispersed or segregate into secondary phases.
generation.mechanism: Under rapid synthesis conditions, the very limited mobility of atoms forces the particle formation to follow a stochastic process where the low concentration of each element statistically suppresses local ordering or clustering. When the dwell time is extended, the additional thermal energy allows atoms to overcome kinetic barriers to migrate, thereby enabling local segregation and phase separation that are normally inhibited in the rapid process.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline process that yields single-phase, uniformly mixed HEA nanoparticles, the controlled extension of the dwell time will lead to signs of elemental segregation, the appearance of secondary phases (or intermetallic compounds), and possibly less uniform particle morphology. This altered microstructure would directly indicate that increased atomic mobility alters the phase selection.
generation.baseline: Single-phase, randomly mixed HEA nanoparticles produced by rapid heating (e.g., 55-ms pulse) and ultra-fast cooling that kinetically trap the high-entropy solid solution across all constituent elements.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to systems with more than five noble metals processed from solid precursors under non-equilibrium conditions. It holds when the synthesis conditions strictly enforce minimal atomic mobility (very short dwell times and high cooling rates). Deviations from these boundaries (e.g., longer dwell times or conditions that promote atom diffusion) would lead to phase separation.
generation.uncertainty: The exact dwell time threshold at which the onset of segregation occurs may depend on the specific elemental combinations and detailed processing conditions; further experiments are needed to pinpoint this critical value.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of noble metal HEA nanoparticles under identical conditions except for the dwell time at the peak temperature. One set uses the standard rapid synthesis (e.g., 55-ms dwell time) and the other uses an extended dwell time (e.g., a few seconds) while maintaining the same peak temperature and cooling rates. Perform detailed phase and elemental analyses (using X-ray diffraction, TEM, and EDS mapping) on both sets.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the extended dwell time does not result in any significant increase in phase separation or elemental segregation compared to the baseline rapid synthesis, then the hypothesis—that limited atomic mobility promotes stochastic single-phase formation—would be called into question.

cited_evidence.text: This simple model of particle formation demonstrates that adding more elements innately promotes a more random nanoparticle, regardless of element interactions. Naturally, this model offers an idealized perspective and does not reflect all experimental details. In reality, there will be distinct mixing enthalpies between the elements. This will introduce a preference for certain structures which is opposed by the limited mobility of atoms. This explains how a rather mixed particle is obtained in the synthesis for a five-element mixture, which is restricted in the binary case, but also sees signs of local segregation in the NMF analysis. The model relates well to the single-source precursor synthesis, where a solid precursor is reduced at moderate temperatures, hence limiting the free mobility. Extending this approach to other syntheses with similar solid, mixed precursors can thus provide a viable way to design new low-temperature approaches for small high entropy alloy nanoparticles. Simultaneous in situ X-ray diffraction and multi-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy experiments allowed us to study the formation mechanism of noble metal bimetallic and high entropy alloy nanoparticles in depth. The samples were prepared by reduction of single-source precursors. For five-element mixtures, the formation of a single phase occurs more readily than in the binary samples. Under the studied reaction conditions, single-phase formation for binary alloys was restricted to systems where cooperative reduction occurred, while single-phase HEA particles could be obtained even though the elements were reduced consecutively. The findings are explained with a stochastic model that simulates the particle formation process. Regardless of the element interactions, the model quantifies that it is more likely to form a random alloy if more atom types are present in a system with limited free atom mobility. This highlights that knowledge of the formation mechanism is crucial for understanding the material formation pathways. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) contain five or more principal elements in equimolar or near-equimolar ratios. When the size of HEAs decreases to nanoscale, such as nanoparticles, the high specific surface area, quantum size effect, strong synergistic interaction, and lattice distortion make them an ideal platform for a variety of surface reactions, showing great promise for a wide range of emerging energy-related applications, particularly in the field of catalysis. There are two categories of methods for the preparation of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (HEA NPs), generally classified as the “top-down” physical methods by crushing bulk materials and the “bottom-up” chemical methods by reducing metal salt precursors. The HEA NPs prepared by ball milling usually display a large distribution in the composition. Wet chemical synthesis can effectively control the composition, phase structure, and particle size of the target elements.
